1.pericope_label: And the LORD spake unto Moses and Aaron in the land of Egypt, saying, This month shall be unto you the beginning of months: it shall be the first month of the year to you. Speak ye unto all the congregation of Israel, saying, In the tenth day of this month they shall take to them every man a lamb, according to the house of their fathers, a lamb for an house

schools.summary: Gill argues the words were spoken before the firstborn were slain and probably before the three days’ darkness, since the command must have preceded the passover by four days; he would render the opening as the Lord had spoken, and holds the account was deferred to this place so the history of the plagues should not be interrupted. He supplies an agricultural check on the month, that Abib means an ear of corn and the barley was then in ear. Calvin asks why, if one Lamb alone reconciled the Church, a lamb should be slain in every house, and answers that though all were protected by the same blood God would have each family separately reminded so as to feel the grace peculiarly conferred on itself, as baptism is one yet conferred on every individual; the joining of neighbours he explains by the rule that nothing be left, lest the sacred feast be mixed with daily food, or superstition arise from the remnants, for which cause the bones too were burnt.

Henry states the calendar change in round terms, from the middle of September to the middle of March, at least in all ecclesiastical computations, and finds it good to begin the day, the year, and especially our lives with God.

Clarke states the common view that God now moved the year’s commencement from Tisri, the month in which the Jews suppose the world was created with the earth appearing at once in all its fruits, to Abib, producing the twofold civil and sacred reckoning; but he then reports Houbigant’s objection with approval as plausible, that no new commencement is noted here at all, since the year had always begun in this month and the words shall be have nothing answering to them in the Hebrew, so that the verse is a statement rather than a decree, marking the month only so that posterity might know when to keep the passover. On the interval he notes that in later times preparation began on the thirteenth, but that this first occasion required more time amid very great confusion, and passes on Ainsworth’s observations that Israel crossed Jordan on this day of the month and that Christ entered Jerusalem on it. Wesley follows Henry on the change of year.

Keil reads in the land of Egypt as connecting this law with the giving of the law at Sinai, and explains that a divine consecration was needed so that the outward severance from Egypt might be matched by an inward severance from everything heathen, the feast laying the foundation of Israel’s birth into a new life of grace; he explains all the congregation as the nation represented by its elders, and reckoning by fathers’ houses as the natural distribution into families so that only one household circle should unite. Ellicott records that the Hebrews had begun with Tisri near the autumnal equinox, following neither the Egyptian year beginning in June with the Nile’s rise nor the Babylonian beginning at the vernal equinox, that henceforth they kept two years so that the first civil month was the seventh sacred, and that the month was still called Abib, the month of greenness. He explains the four days’ interval as allowing careful inspection for blemish, and notes that the word rendered lamb applies equally to sheep and goats, that only lambs seem practically ever to have been offered, and that the command presupposes a society without extreme poverty, every Israelite able to own or buy one.

debates: Whether the verse institutes a new calendar or merely identifies an existing month: Clarke reports Houbigant’s argument from the absence of any verb in the Hebrew as plausible, while Ellicott describes the change as a real one and reconstructs both the old and the new reckoning.
outliers: Calvin turns a ritual detail into a question about the individual application of a single atonement, and answers it from the practice of baptism.
Ellicott infers a social fact from the command, that a society in which every household can supply a lamb has no extreme poverty in it.

4.pericope_label: And if the household be too little for the lamb, let him and his neighbour next unto his house take it according to the number of the souls. Your lamb shall be without blemish, a male of the first year: ye shall take it out from the sheep, or from the goats: and ye shall keep it up until the fourteenth day of the same month: and the whole assembly of the congregation of Israel shall kill it in the evening

schools.summary: Gill reports that Maimonides reckons no fewer than fifty blemishes any one of which makes a creature unfit, and takes the keeping up of the lamb as a type of the preservation of Christ in his infancy until the appointed time. Calvin reads the perfection as a measure of what was needed: the expiation was not legitimate unless it possessed the utmost perfection, such as is never found in men, so that Israel might learn that propitiating God required a more excellent price than the whole human race could furnish, and since such excellency could much less exist in a beast, the celestial purity of Christ was shown forth by the lamb’s visible perfection. He then declines an allegory his tradition offered, preferring to be ignorant why the flesh was roasted and not boiled rather than invent such unfounded subtleties as that Christ was in a manner roasted on the cross.

Clarke gives the rabbinic bounds of ten to twenty persons for a lamb, reports the reckoning of fifty blemishes and despises it as trifling most egregiously, itemising five in the ear, three in the eyelid, eight in the eye, three in the nose and six in the mouth, and glosses a male of the first year as any age between eight days and twelve months. He notes the Hebrews generally preferred the lamb to the kid, lists the four things the rabbins say were required at the first passover only — eating it in houses dispersed through Goshen, taking the lamb on the tenth, striking the blood on the posts, and eating in haste — observes that any person might kill it, the sacrificial act not being confined to the priests, and explains between the two evenings as the span from noon to sunset and from sunset through twilight, remarking with approval that God sets no particular hour.

Keil takes the clause literally as the house being too small for a lamb and explains that families were to estimate how much each person would eat, so that more than two might unite; he rejects the gloss that a male of the first year means any age from the eighth day to the year’s end, that rule belonging to other sacrifices, and calls quite erroneous the opinion that oxen were admitted later, denying it can be proved from the passages cited. On the four days’ interval he canvasses Jonathan and Rashi, who restricted it to the Egyptian passover, Fagius, whose reason that the sight of the lamb would prompt conversation about the deliverance he grants has some truth but says hardly explains exactly four days, and Hoffmann, whose reference to the four generations depends on the lamb being a sacrifice, which Hoffmann himself denies without sufficient reason. Ellicott describes the joining of households as two small families clubbing or a large one drafting off members, corrects the English to shall ye count, gives Josephus’ bounds of ten to twenty, appeals to natural piety against offering the blind, lame or sick, holds males especially appropriate as representing the firstborn male of each house, gives the age as not above a year old on the ground that animals like children were thought most innocent when young, and explains the four days as custody allowing thorough inspection.

debates: What a male of the first year means: Clarke allows any age from eight days to twelve months, while Keil rejects that reading as belonging to other sacrifices and Ellicott gives simply not above a year old.
Why the lamb was taken four days early: Keil weighs and finds fault with three explanations, while Ellicott settles for inspection.
outliers: Calvin explicitly refuses a typological reading available to him, saying he would rather be ignorant of why the flesh was roasted than invent the subtlety that Christ was roasted on the cross.
Clarke and Gill report the same rabbinic tally of fifty blemishes, Gill neutrally and Clarke as an example of egregious trifling.

7.pericope_label: And they shall take of the blood, and strike it on the two side posts and on the upper door post of the houses, wherein they shall eat it. And they shall eat the flesh in that night, roast with fire, and unleavened bread; and with bitter herbs they shall eat it. And thus shall ye eat it; with your loins girded, your shoes on your feet, and your staff in your hand; and ye shall eat it in haste: it is the LORD’S passover

schools.summary: Gill canvasses three readings of the prohibition of raw flesh — Jarchi and Maimonides taking it of flesh the fire has begun to work on but not enough for eating, others deriving the word from a root meaning to break so that it forbids cutting the animal up, and Abarbinel taking it in the ordinary sense of now, which Gill dismisses as needless since they had already been told to keep the lamb till the fourteenth. He turns the rule that nothing remain typologically, that a whole Christ is to be received and fed upon by faith, and reports the Targum of Jonathan’s note that these rites belonged to this time and not to ages following.

Clarke supplies Ainsworth’s reason for leaving the threshold unsmeared, to teach a reverent regard for the blood of Christ so that men should not tread under foot the Son of God; suggests the command to roast was aimed at the Egyptians who ate raw flesh in honour of Osiris, adding that the Ethiopians are still remarkable for it; explains the inclusion of the inward parts by the heathen use of them for divination, impossible once roasted this way; argues that the heathen sacrifice called propter viam, offered before a journey and eaten whole with the remainder burned, was borrowed from the passover, retailing Cato’s jibe from Macrobius against a man who burned his house because he had eaten everything else; gives prevention of putrefaction as the reason nothing was to remain, since what is offered to God should not see corruption, as the Lord’s body did not; and explains the travelling dress from Chardin, the loose eastern garment tucked into the girdle and shoes mentioned precisely because easterns remove them to eat, sitting cross-legged in backless slippers on carpets. Wesley glosses raw as half roasted rather than thoroughly dressed.

Keil observes that the posts and lintel surrounded the door and that the doorway stood for the house itself, as in thy gates stands for in thy towns, and notes that the threshold was excluded though it belongs to the door as much as the lintel; he settles that the Hebrew behind boiled means to become done rather than to be boiled, follows Rashi in taking the animal undivided with no bone broken and the viscera roasted inside once cleansed, and glosses the phrase for haste as anxious flight. Ellicott derives the word for the upper door post from a root meaning to look out, making it properly the latticed window above the door through which callers were reconnoitred, a feature frequent on early Egyptian monuments, so that blood there would show atonement made for the inmates; he gives practical reasons for roasting, the simplest and most primitive mode and the only one open to all since most would lack a cauldron large enough; reports from Justin Martyr the two wooden spits that extended the lamb on a sort of cross; explains the burning of remnants as guarding against profanation or superstitious use, comparing his own church’s rule for the eucharistic elements; and states that the travelling injunctions were never repeated in the law nor held binding at any later passover.

debates: Why nothing was to remain until morning: Clarke gives prevention of putrefaction, Ellicott the prevention of profanation or superstitious use of the remnants.
Why roasting was commanded: Clarke reads it as a polemic against Egyptian practice, Ellicott as the only method available to households without large cauldrons.
outliers: Clarke argues that a Roman sacrifice before a journey was borrowed from the passover, and illustrates it with a joke of Cato’s preserved in Macrobius.
Ellicott identifies the upper door post as a latticed observation window known from Egyptian monuments, making the blood a public sign rather than a private mark.

12.pericope_label: For I will pass through the land of Egypt this night, and will smite all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, both man and beast; and against all the gods of Egypt I will execute judgment: I am the LORD. And the blood shall be to you for a token upon the houses where ye are: and when I see the blood, I will pass over you. And this day shall be unto you for a memorial; and ye shall keep it a feast to the LORD throughout your generations

schools.summary: Gill makes the blood a sign both to the Israelites that the Lord would make good his promises and to the destroying angel not to enter, and reports the Jewish saying that as Israel was redeemed in Nisan, in Nisan they will be redeemed again. Calvin holds that God declares himself judge against the false gods because it then especially appeared how utterly unable they were to help and how vain and fallacious their service was, and that he would conquer not only the nation but its very gods, dismissing the rabbinic account as tame and far-fetched; on the perpetual ordinance he admits perpetuity is meant but only such as would last until the renovation of the Church, as with circumcision and the whole ceremonial law, since by Christ’s coming it was abolished in use yet only then attained its true solidity, the new covenant destroying the old not in substance but in form.

Clarke works through three answers to the threat against the gods of Egypt and rejects two: the sacred animals, which he finds not very clear or satisfactory; the marginal princes, which he answers by asking why some should be distinguished in a calamity that fell on all Egyptian families alike; and Houbigant’s emendation of gods to tents or habitations, two letters having been interchanged, which he calls simple and natural and which would threaten every dwelling in Egypt. He then undercuts his own preference, granting that however probable the criticism appears it has no support from any ancient version or from the manuscripts collated by Kennicott and De Rossi, and that the parallel passage tells against it, and closes with the principle that a conquered nation’s gods were always supposed to have abandoned it or been overcome. He calls the ordinance endless because representative of the Lamb of God, and observes that though Jewish sacrifice has wholly ceased the passover and unleavened bread are still kept everywhere, with no lamb offered and the flesh partly roasted and partly boiled so as not to resemble the primitive sacrifice, since it is held unlawful to sacrifice outside Jerusalem.

Ellicott holds gods far preferable to princes, since some Egyptian sacred animals were regarded as actual incarnations of deity, and since cows, goats, cats, dogs, jackals, crocodiles, hippopotami, apes, ibises and frogs were sacred in Egypt or parts of it, so that a general destruction of firstborn animals would be felt as a blow to the gods almost equally; he prefers go through to pass through, the verb being entirely unconnected with the word behind passover, reverses the direction of the token so that the blood is a sign to God on Israel’s behalf, and makes the ordinance’s continuation concrete in the Eucharist and in an Easter celebration corresponding exactly in time. Keil takes the blood as a sign and pledge that Jehovah would spare them, cautions against rendering the last clause for the destroyer since the noun lacks the article, and grounds the perpetuity in proportion: an act of redemption of eternal significance requires a commemoration upheld as long as Israel exists as the redeemed people.

debates: What the gods of Egypt are: Clarke rejects both the sacred-animal and the princes readings and leans to Houbigant’s emendation to tents while conceding it has no manuscript support, where Ellicott defends the sacred animals at length and Calvin takes the gods as powerless deities publicly exposed.
Whom the blood signals: Gill and Clarke make it a sign to the destroying angel, Ellicott a token presented to God on Israel’s behalf.
How far for ever extends: Clarke makes it endless in this world and the next, Calvin limits it to the renovation of the Church, Ellicott transfers it to the Eucharist and Easter.
outliers: Clarke argues for a textual emendation and then supplies the evidence against it himself, leaving the reading unsettled.
Clarke notes an observable consequence, that the modern passover meal is deliberately cooked so as not to resemble a sacrifice.

15.pericope_label: Seven days shall ye eat unleavened bread; even the first day ye shall put away leaven out of your houses: for whosoever eateth leavened bread from the first day until the seventh day, that soul shall be cut off from Israel. And in the first day there shall be an holy convocation, and in the seventh day there shall be an holy convocation to you; no manner of work shall be done in them

schools.summary: Calvin explains why so severe a penalty attaches to so small a thing: abstaining from leaven may be in itself a trifling matter, as Paul teaches that bodily exercise profiteth little, yet since in this ceremony the redemption of the people was kept in memory it was a very gross crime not to observe whatever God had prescribed, for we must estimate the importance of the rites of the law from their object. Gill holds the seven days of unleavened bread a distinct festival which does not concern the first passover at all, since the Israelites then ate unleavened bread of necessity, having no other, and did so for thirty days after; the commanded feast came later, commemorating a departure so hasty they had no time to leaven the dough in their troughs. He reports that on the fourteenth the most diligent search was made for leaven, whatever was found being burnt, cast into the sea or dispersed with the wind.

Clarke likewise makes the ordinance distinct and not essentially connected with the passover, the one on the fourteenth and the other from the fifteenth for seven days, of which the first and last were holy convocations. On being cut off he counts thirty-six places where the excision is threatened, says what is implied is not well known — some think a violent death, some premature, some eternal — and himself takes it as no more than separation from the rights and privileges of an Israelite, leaving the man a stranger with neither lot nor part in Israel, and probably inflicted only on those showing marked and obstinate contempt for divine authority; he adds that this appears nearly the same as Christian excommunication, from which the Christian usage seems borrowed. He calls this the first account anywhere of an assembly collected for the mere purpose of religious worship, and notes that the Hebrew word answers to the Greek term we translate Church, an assembly convened by public call. He describes the later search for leaven, every part of the house swept so that not a crumb remain, and the rule that if even a mouse was seen crossing the floor with a crumb in its mouth the whole house was held polluted and the purification begun afresh, leaven being an emblem of sin because it proceeds from corruption. Wesley glosses convocation as a solemn day to assemble, and stranger as a proselyte.

Keil dates the instruction from the words I brought out, holding that Moses did not receive the directions about the seven days until after the exodus and that they stand here only for their internal connection with the passover, and reconciles the first day with the fourteenth at even by that same connection, unleavened bread being eaten with the lamb. He rejects Vitringa’s rendering of holy convocation as a proclamation of sanctity, giving a holy assembly for the worship of Jehovah, and notes that work necessary for preparing food was permitted here though forbidden on the Sabbath, whence the later term servile work. Ellicott adds that the summons appears to have been made by the silver trumpets and that the people gathered at the door of the sanctuary; on the stranger he explains a foreigner in blood adopted by circumcision as a full proselyte, thinks many of the six hundred thousand were such, and answers the charge of Hebrew exclusiveness by noting that the privileges were open from the first to those who accepted circumcision, as the Kenites and even the Gibeonites did; the contrasting phrase he renders natives of the land, meaning a Canaan reckoned Abraham’s from the first promise, so that his descendants were its expatriated inhabitants.

debates: When the seven-day feast was commanded: Keil argues from the past tense of I brought out that the instruction postdates the exodus and is placed here only by association, while Gill and Clarke treat it simply as a later institution distinct from the passover.
What being cut off entails: Clarke reports three views — violent, premature, and eternal death — and adopts a fourth, civil separation from Israel.
outliers: Ellicott uses the clause about the stranger to answer a modern charge of exclusiveness, arguing that the covenant was open to any foreigner who accepted circumcision.
Clarke traces Christian excommunication genealogically to this penalty, and the word Church to the Hebrew term for convocation.

21.pericope_label: Then Moses called for all the elders of Israel, and said unto them, Draw out and take you a lamb according to your families, and kill the passover. And ye shall take a bunch of hyssop, and dip it in the blood that is in the bason, and strike the lintel and the two side posts with the blood; and none of you shall go out at the door of his house until the morning

schools.summary: Gill reports the whole range of proposed plants and adds a practical observation, that rosemary seems fitter to strike or sprinkle with than hyssop, while granting that hyssop is generally understood because the Hebrew word is so near in sound; he passes on Jarchi’s rule that three stalks make a bunch, and notes that the heathens sprinkled with laurel or olive branches. He limits the perpetual clause to the feasts and their rites rather than the sprinkling, which was peculiar to Egypt. Calvin makes the command to stay indoors a matter of separation, lest they mix with the Egyptians and be exposed to destruction outside the safeguard of the blood; he holds the destroyer an angel delegated by God and, though God often uses evil angels, gathers from other passages that this was one of the elect angels who also ministered the people’s deliverance; and on the duty of teaching he calls doctrine the life of sacraments, without which no vigour remains in them, arguing that since the paschal lamb corresponds with the Holy Supper, none can be duly admitted to receive it but those capable of being taught.

Henry gives two reasons for the command to stay indoors: that they must not straggle and be out of the way when summoned to depart, and that since the destroying angel could perfectly well have told an Israelite from an Egyptian in the street, the command was meant to intimate that their safety was owing to the blood of sprinkling.

Clarke lists the renderings offered for the plant — musk, rosemary, polypody of the wall, mint, origanum, marjoram and hyssop — prefers the last, derives its name from Parkhurst as denoting detersive and cleansing qualities, and describes it botanically as an undershrub with spear-shaped opposite leaves and whorled spikes of flowers, aromatic and pungent and recommended in disorders of the breast and lungs, supposing that its medicinal qualities were probably why it was so particularly recommended in Scripture. Wesley refuses to decide the destroyer’s nature: whether this was a good or an evil angel, we have not light to determine.

Keil doubts the hyssop identification on geographical grounds, since it is uncertain whether the officinal plant grows in Syria and Arabia at all, and prefers a species of origanum, the Arabian zater, wild marjoram or a kind of thyme, very common there; he takes the bason as the vessel that caught the blood, notes that ordinary purifications sprinkled rather than struck with the bunch, gives the plain reason for staying indoors that there was no safety on such a night except behind the blood-stained door, and identifies the destroyer with the angel of Jehovah in whom God revealed himself to the patriarchs, expressly denying he was a fallen angel and reconciling the psalm’s angels of evil by referring it to the pestilence as well. Ellicott names the caper plant, called asaf by the Arabs and plentiful in the Sinaitic region, as the likeliest candidate; he notes that the word rendered bason also means threshold and was so taken by the Greek and Latin, that the article is difficult on either reading since neither had been mentioned, and argues against the threshold that blood on it would have made the lintel and doorposts unnecessary; he holds that Moses gave the command to stay indoors on his own authority without positive divine direction; and he rules out any struggle between Jehovah and the destroyer, against Bishop Lowth and Redslob, the destroyer being simply his minister.

debates: What plant is meant: Clarke argues for hyssop proper, Keil for an Arabian origanum or thyme on the ground that hyssop may not grow there, Ellicott for the caper plant, while Gill notes that rosemary would in fact sprinkle better.
Whether the word means bason or threshold: Ellicott reports that the Greek and Latin chose threshold and argues against it from the redundancy it would create.
What the destroyer was: Calvin makes him an elect angel, Keil the angel of Jehovah, Ellicott simply a minister with no opposition to God, and Wesley declines to say.
outliers: Ellicott holds that one of the chapter’s commands, that none go out of doors, was issued by Moses on his own authority rather than by divine direction.
Calvin turns the instruction to teach children into a rule of sacramental admission, excluding from the Supper any who cannot be taught.

25.pericope_label: And it shall come to pass, when ye be come to the land which the LORD will give you, according as he hath promised, that ye shall keep this service. And it shall come to pass, when your children shall say unto you, What mean ye by this service? That ye shall say, It is the sacrifice of the LORD’S passover, who passed over the houses of the children of Israel in Egypt. And the people bowed the head and worshipped

schools.summary: Gill divides the sacrifice in two, eucharistical by way of thanksgiving for their safety when the firstborn of the Egyptians were slain, and propitiatory, the blood atoning for all within the house where it was sprinkled, which he takes from Aben Ezra, and typical of the atoning sacrifice of Christ; he notes that the elders then departed to their several tribes and families. Calvin makes the proclamation a condition of the sign’s validity, since without it the rite would be an empty and unmeaning proceeding, and God would have fathers proclaim it to their children so that the knowledge of their redemption, handed down by tradition, may flourish in all ages; he corrects the rendering work to worship, since in many passages to serve God means to worship him, and reads the people’s bowing as a correction of past ingratitude, since they had professed obedience before but with little constancy, being so harassed by their afflictions as to neglect their duty, and now gave actual proof by diligently performing whatever was commanded.

Clarke calls the annual service a very wise provision for keeping the deliverance in remembrance, and notes that from the remotest antiquity feasts and games have preserved the memory of grand events, the Sabbath keeping the creation in mind as the passover keeps the deliverance. He reports from Calmet that the Jews never took their sons to the temple before twelve years of age nor let them eat the flesh of any victim until they had themselves offered a sacrifice there, and that Joseph and Mary took the child at this age, probably for the first time. He then sets out a chain of observations: the anniversary was kept on the very day and hour throughout all generations; on one of these anniversaries, many suppose on the very hour, Christ expired; after the destruction of Jerusalem the lamb ceased to be offered anywhere though the anniversary is still held without sacrifice; the Lord’s Supper was instituted to keep the true paschal sacrifice in commemoration and has been observed by the whole Christian world, one very small class excepted; and as the Jews were commanded to eat the lamb, so Christ commanded his disciples to take and eat. He concludes that the words about an ordinance for ever are literally fulfilled, the lamb being the significator until the passion and bread and wine thereafter until the end of the world. Wesley reads the bowing as signifying submission to the institution as a law and thankfulness for it as a favour and privilege.

Ellicott renders the answer as this is a passover-sacrifice to Jehovah, observes that the emphatic word is passover and that it was the meaning of this term which was especially to be explained, and notes that the explanation would necessarily involve an historical account of the circumstances of the institution, apt to call forth gratitude and devotion. Keil reads the people’s obedience as appropriation, that they proceeded to execute the command so that through the obedience of faith they might make the blessing of this service their own.

debates: What the prescribed answer is chiefly about: Ellicott makes the term passover itself the thing to be explained, while Gill divides the answer into a eucharistic and a propitiatory account of the sacrifice.
outliers: Clarke argues that the passover survives literally as an ordinance for ever by transfer to the Eucharist, and notes in passing that one very small class of Christians does not observe it.
Calvin insists that a sign without its accompanying proclamation is empty, making the duty of teaching constitutive of the rite rather than an addition to it.

29.pericope_label: And it came to pass, that at midnight the LORD smote all the firstborn in the land of Egypt, from the firstborn of Pharaoh that sat on his throne unto the firstborn of the captive that was in the dungeon; and there was a great cry in Egypt; for there was not a house where there was not one dead. And he called for Moses and Aaron by night, and said, Rise up, and get you forth from among my people; and bless me also

schools.summary: Gill notes that the Egyptians were fast asleep and thoughtless of any danger, that Pharaoh sent servants rather than going himself since he never saw Moses’ face again, and that he at last concedes the flocks and herds he had refused. Calvin thinks it not probable that God’s servants were recalled into Pharaoh’s presence, holding that he is said to have called them when by sending his chief courtiers he compelled their departure, which the context proves since the Egyptians immediately urged them out in haste, and adding that there is nothing absurd in saying Pharaoh called a man he had threatened with death when he sent his nobles with the command. He finds the whole speech a portrait of an alarmed and anxious person, now taking no less precaution against delay than he had before been diligent in bargaining, the change betraying itself since the same God who had hardened his iron heart has now broken it.

Henry makes the hour part of the blow, the three preceding nights having been made dreadful by a darkness that might be felt, so that the alarm came when they hoped for one quiet night’s rest, and contrasts it with the later plague at Jerusalem which fell by day and was for that reason less frightful. He takes the stroke by parts: it fell on the firstborn, the joy and hope of their families, measure for measure since they had slain the Hebrews’ children; it reached from the throne to the dungeon, prince and peasant standing on the same level before God’s judgments; and the cry was universal, since the Egyptians could have no help from neighbours all involved in the same calamity. With Wesley he argues that Pharaoh sent them out not as men hated, as the pagan historians have represented, but as men feared, which his humble request for a blessing plainly discovers.

Clarke supplies the ethnography behind the cry, that no people were more remarkable for their mournings than the Egyptians, who whipped, beat and tore themselves and howled in all the excess of grief, the household leaving the house on a death and howling in the streets in the most lamentable and frantic manner; he notes that Herodotus was once in Egypt at one of their solemnities and saw myriads beating themselves so. He agrees that Pharaoh sent a message rather than summoning Moses in person. Wesley reads the surrender as fear rather than hatred, noting that those who set God at defiance will seek him in their distress.

Keil says the stroke fell when all Egypt lay in deep sleep, to startle king and people out of their sleep of sin, and weighs whether it had a natural basis like the previous plagues, since the analogy of the pestilence in David’s day might suggest pestilence as the means, the miracle then lying in the sudden death of the firstborn of man and beast alone while the Israelites remained uninjured. Alone among these voices he holds that Pharaoh really did send for Moses and Aaron, denying that this is at variance with the earlier threat and that there is any necessity for Calvin’s explanation, since a command never to appear in his sight again did not preclude sending for them under totally different circumstances. Ellicott denies that the clause about every house can be literally true, since in half the families a daughter would have opened the womb and in others the firstborn son would have been absent or already dead, and argues that to judge Scripture fairly we must allow for the hyperbole of Oriental expression, which substitutes universal terms for general ones; the meaning is that in the great majority of houses there was one dead, which may well be so if dependants and the pet animals that abounded in Egyptian homes are included. On the last clause he calls it the extreme point of Pharaoh’s humiliation, that he must crave a blessing from men he had driven from his presence under threat of death.

debates: Whether Pharaoh summoned Moses in person: Calvin, Clarke and Ellicott all take the calling to have been done through officials, since Pharaoh had sworn never to see him again, while Keil insists the text means what it says and that the oath did not bind him under wholly changed circumstances.
Whether not a house without one dead is literal: Ellicott argues it cannot be and defends the text as Oriental hyperbole, where the others report the clause without qualification.
outliers: Keil entertains a natural mechanism for the plague, locating the miracle in its selectivity rather than in the means.
Ellicott counts pet animals among the dead to make the universal clause defensible.

33.pericope_label: And the Egyptians were urgent upon the people, that they might send them out of the land in haste; for they said, We be all dead men. And the people took their dough before it was leavened, their kneadingtroughs being bound up in their clothes upon their shoulders. And the children of Israel journeyed from Rameses to Succoth, about six hundred thousand on foot that were men, beside children. And a mixed multitude went up also with them; and flocks, and herds, even very much cattle

schools.summary: Gill lists four motives for the mixed multitude — intermarriage, religion in the case of proselytes of righteousness, worldly interest since Egypt was now desolate, and the judgment that a people so favoured of heaven were the safest company — and adds the Targum of Jonathan’s figure of two hundred and forty myriads. He raises a practical difficulty about the baking, Succoth being a desert where ovens could hardly be had, and answers that the cakes might be laid on coals and frequently turned or covered under hot ashes. Calvin approaches the crowd from an accounting problem: since Moses mentions no servants at the descent into Egypt and Jacob could hardly maintain more than his own children through the famine, they brought no great number down, so the mixed multitude were either Egypt’s own offspring or migrants drawn there as fertile lands attract strangers; he notes the same expression later, where the mixed multitude was separated lest the Church be polluted by a confused admixture, and answers the objection that ungodly men would not forsake a rich habitation by observing that Egypt had been so afflicted that its very poverty might drive its inhabitants away.

Henry supposes the greatest part of the mixed multitude were a rude unthinking mob that followed the crowd they knew not why, and that on learning of the forty years they quitted and returned; there were always those among the Israelites, he concludes, that were not Israelites, and there are still hypocrites in the church. He reckons the women and children at twice the six hundred thousand men, and marvels at the increase from seventy souls in little more than two hundred years.

Clarke says the Egyptians felt much and feared more, wishing to be rid of a people on whose account they had been smitten with so many plagues, and describes the vessels from modern usage, the kneading troughs of the Arabs being small wooden bowls that afterwards serve as dishes, suggesting that bound up in their clothes may mean no more than wrapped in the long loose garment the Arabs call a hyke, a blanket like a highland plaid. Wesley draws the moral that when death comes into our houses it is seasonable to think of our own mortality, and alone declines the object altogether, holding that the word means not kneading troughs but the lumps of unleavened paste themselves.

Ellicott observes that not Pharaoh only but the Egyptian nation generally was anxious for an immediate departure and expedited it in every way, which facilitated their all setting forth at once and accounts for their readiness to part with jewels and raiment; he corrects lent to gave, since the Egyptians neither expected nor wished them to return, agrees with Clarke on the bowls, and is the most candid about the mixed multitude, saying nothing is told us of its component elements though some may have been Egyptians impressed by the miracles and some foreigners glad to escape servitude, and noting that Egyptian writers in their perverted accounts of the exodus made a multitude of foreigners take part with the Hebrews. He describes the Arab way of baking, attaching round pieces of dough to the inside of a heated oven. Keil explains that the urgency forced them to take the dough unleavened and the troughs bound in a large square cloth worn over the under-clothes, adds that they had meant to leaven it since the seven days’ command had not yet been given, takes the word for the multitude as literally a mixture or swarm of foreigners, treats their coming as a typical fulfilment of the promise that all families should be blessed in Abraham, and notes that they occupied a very low position as hewers of wood and drawers of water whom Israel could not shake off.

debates: What the word rendered kneadingtroughs denotes: Clarke, Ellicott and Keil all take it of a vessel, while Wesley holds it means the lumps of unleavened paste themselves.

Who the mixed multitude were: Ellicott says nothing is known, Gill lists four motives, Keil makes them a fulfilment of the Abrahamic promise, Henry a rude mob and a standing type of hypocrites in the church.
outliers: Ellicott notes that Egyptian writers themselves recorded a body of foreigners leaving with the Hebrews, using a hostile source as corroboration.
Calvin argues backwards from the silence about Jacob’s servants to conclude that the mixed multitude must have been recruited in Egypt.

40.pericope_label: Now the sojourning of the children of Israel, who dwelt in Egypt, was four hundred and thirty years. And it came to pass at the end of the four hundred and thirty years, even the selfsame day it came to pass, that all the hosts of the LORD went out from the land of Egypt. It is a night to be much observed unto the LORD for bringing them out from the land of Egypt

schools.summary: Gill reports the expansions of the verse found in the Greek, the Samaritan, both Talmuds and Aben Ezra, all adding Canaan or the other lands, and states flatly that Israel did not dwell in Egypt four hundred and thirty years, nor much more than two hundred. He takes the phrase about the night as a night of observations, in which many things are to be marked to the honour and glory of God. Calvin agrees that the period cannot begin from Jacob’s descent, since it is very clear from other passages that from Jacob’s entry to the exodus not more than two hundred and thirty years at most had passed; and he reads the command about the night as a safeguard against decay, the admonition being useful so that the Israelites should retain the legitimate use of the feast and it might not grow into a mere cold ceremony, as is often the case, adding that the generations of the ancient people were ended by the coming of Christ, the shadows of the law ceasing when the state of the Church was renewed and the Gentiles gathered into the same body.

Clarke calls the statement extremely difficult on all hands and reports Kennicott’s survey: the descendants of Israel demonstrably did not dwell so long in Egypt, extending Egypt to include Canaan will not close the gap, and stretching the children of Israel to cover Israel himself, Isaac, and part of Abraham’s life reaches the exact sum but by a method that might arrive at anything but truth, which was never thus conveyed by an inspired writer. His own answer is textual: the Samaritan Pentateuch reads that the sojourning of the children of Israel and of their fathers in Canaan and in Egypt was four hundred and thirty years, the Alexandrian Greek agrees, and Paul gives the same sum reckoning from the promise to Abraham, so that two clauses have dropped out of the present Hebrew; he checks it by arithmetic, twenty-five years from Abraham’s entry to Isaac’s birth, sixty to Jacob’s, a hundred and thirty to the descent, and two hundred and fifteen in Egypt. He calls the night one to be held in everlasting remembrance. Wesley sets the two passover nights side by side, the first much to be observed and the last, in which Christ was betrayed, much more, when a yoke heavier than Egypt’s was broken and a better land than Canaan set before us — a temporal deliverance against an eternal redemption to be celebrated world without end.

Ellicott alone defends the plain Hebrew, rendering the clause as which they sojourned in Egypt and supporting it twice over: by the prophecy that Abraham’s seed should be a stranger in a land not theirs and serve them four hundred years, which he takes of Egypt and not Canaan, and by the genealogy of Joshua, which places him in the eleventh generation from Jacob and accords well with this term of years, the other genealogies being more or less abbreviated. He takes the selfsame day to mean that all started on one day, though some by night, some in the morning and others later, having different distances to traverse to the appointed halt. Keil denies that the rare word for the night means celebration, from a root signifying to observe or honour, as Knobel held, and gives preservation, from a root meaning to keep, so that the night was consecrated to the Lord as a preservation for all Israel in their families because he had preserved them from the destroyer.

debates: How long Israel was in Egypt: Clarke, Gill and Calvin all shorten the Egyptian sojourn to about two hundred years and lengthen the reckoning back to Abraham, Clarke on the authority of the Samaritan text, the Alexandrian Greek and Paul; Ellicott alone keeps the plain Hebrew and defends four hundred and thirty years in Egypt from prophecy and from Joshua’s genealogy.
What the night is called: Keil rejects Knobel’s celebration for preservation on the strength of the root, while Gill and Clarke read it as a night to be observed and remembered.
outliers: Kennicott, quoted by Clarke, rejects a harmonisation not because it fails but because it succeeds too easily, on the ground that a method able to reach any figure cannot be the one an inspired writer used.

43.pericope_label: And the LORD said unto Moses and Aaron, This is the ordinance of the passover: There shall no stranger eat thereof: but every man’s servant that is bought for money, when thou hast circumcised him, then shall he eat thereof. A foreigner and an hired servant shall not eat thereof

schools.summary: Gill draws the line at proselytes of righteousness, holding that a foreigner or a servant merely hired by the day, week or year was not obliged to circumcision and so had no right to eat. Calvin defends the exclusion as belonging to the nature of a sacrament: the passover was the sacred bond by which God held the elect people in obligation to himself, so a promiscuous permission to eat would have been an unworthy profanation; he notes that among the Gentiles too none but the initiated were admitted to their rites, calls this an absurd imitation of the true ordinance since sacraments are testimonies of God’s special favour to his Church and must not be prostituted to all comers, and describes circumcision as a hedge distinguishing the heathen nations from the holy race of Abraham, adding that God did not refer merely to the outward sign, since all who were circumcised thereby promised to study sincere piety.

Henry runs the rule in both directions. On exclusion he makes it sacramental order, that none might sit at the table but those who came in by the door, and none may now approach the Lord’s supper who have not first submitted to baptism, since we must be born again by the word before we can be nourished by it. On admission he finds an early indication of favour to the Gentiles, a circumcised stranger standing on the same level with the home-born Israelite under one law for both — a mortification to the Jews, teaching them that it was their dedication to God and not their descent from Abraham that entitled them to their privileges — and adds that a master of a household must have all his males circumcised as well as himself.

Clarke argues from the chapter’s last verse that these supplementary rules belonged to the first passover and should be read with the earlier account, and supplies the classification they depend on: all not descended from the sons of Jacob were reputed strangers, and of these there were proselytes of the gate, who would not submit to circumcision though they acknowledged the true God, avoided idolatry and observed the seven precepts of Noah, and proselytes of the covenant, who submitted to circumcision and bound themselves to the whole law. He derives the word rendered foreigner from a root meaning to sit down or dwell, giving a mere sojourner present for traffic and belonging to neither class, and holds the excluded were excluded because they were not under the bond of the covenant and so had no claim on its privileges. Wesley states the condition in five words, unless he submit to be circumcised.

Keil holds that these regulations were not communicated before the exodus at all, since it was only when a crowd of foreigners attached itself to Israel that a connection with foreigners arose needing definition, particularly as regards the festival of Israel’s birth as the people of God. He turns the exclusion into a two-sided principle: because Israel became the people of Jehovah by divine call and not natural descent, no foreigner could share that feast, but because Israel was in that same capacity destined to be a blessing to all nations, the attitude toward foreigners was not to be altogether repelling, so purchased servants already incorporated as Israel’s property were to be entirely incorporated by circumcision. Ellicott distinguishes slaves born in the house, required to be circumcised on the eighth day like Israelites, from bought slaves, who were allowed their choice, and marks what follows: the circumcised slave was admitted to full religious equality with his master. He also notes that the hired servant is assumed to be a foreigner, since otherwise he would of course participate.

debates: When these rules were given: Clarke argues from the closing verse that they belong to the first passover, while Keil holds they were not communicated until after the exodus, when the mixed multitude first made the question of foreigners live.
outliers: Ellicott observes that the rite levelled the household, admitting a circumcised slave to full religious equality with his owner.
Calvin treats pagan mystery initiation as the devil’s counterfeit of sacramental restriction rather than as evidence against it.

46.pericope_label: In one house shall it be eaten; thou shalt not carry forth ought of the flesh abroad out of the house; neither shall ye break a bone thereof. All the congregation of Israel shall keep it. One law shall be to him that is homeborn, and unto the stranger that sojourneth among you. And it came to pass the selfsame day, that the LORD did bring the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt by their armies

schools.summary: Gill allows that more societies than one might eat in a house if they kept distinct and each were large enough for a whole lamb, but insists that one lamb might not be divided between houses, which he takes to denote the unity of the general assembly and the right of each congregation to a whole Christ. Calvin declines certainty about the unbroken bone, offering only that it may have been a further sign of haste, since people at table seldom partake of the marrow except when the meal is protracted, and refusing as too subtle the explanation that the virtue of Christ, represented by the bones, is not diminished while we feed on his flesh; yet he holds that what God commanded concerning the lamb he chose to have openly fulfilled in his Son, treats the soldiers’ restraint at the cross as an interference of providence, and on the closing verses he turns the note of obedience into a note about its author, praising not the people’s promptitude but the power of God in fashioning their hearts and directing their hands, so that in the darkness of the night, amid the greatest disturbances and with nothing well prepared, they were so active and dexterous.

Clarke explains the unbroken bone practically, that haste left no time to separate the bones or break them for marrow, and guesses the flesh was cut off without parting the large joints and the skeleton burnt; he observes that though it was universal custom to break the legs of the crucified, providence so ordered it that a bone of the true paschal Lamb was not broken. He reads one house as one family, or a neighbouring family invited if the first were too small, and connects the ban on carrying the flesh abroad with the command that none leave the house that night. At the word law, its first occurrence, he explains it once for all from a root signifying to aim at, teach, point out, direct or make straight, calling it a system of instruction in righteousness, the fountain of every correct notion of God and the origin of all true principles of law and justice; he draws the political consequence that nations acknowledging this revelation have the most beneficial laws while others have laws at once extravagantly severe and extravagantly indulgent, resting on caprice rather than any weighing of moral turpitude, so that government becomes oppressive and is at length overturned. He closes on the word armies, from a root meaning to assemble in order and thence to war, finding in it the reason God is so often styled the Lord of hosts. Wesley notes that though the passover was observed in families apart it is looked on as the act of the whole congregation, and infers that the Lord’s supper ought not to be neglected by any capable of celebrating it.

Ellicott explains the unbroken bone symbolically: whereas in every other victim the limbs were separated from the body, here the animal was roasted whole and to remain whole, as a symbol of unity and a type of him through whom men are brought into unity with each other and with God. Keil reads the last two verses as hinges, the first closing the instructions with the statement that Israel carried them out in after times and the second closing the account of the exodus, all that Jehovah promised being now fulfilled; and though this is a concluding formula he grants that Abenezra was so far right in wishing to connect it with the following chapter, since such formulae generally link incidents together, winding up what has gone before and introducing what has yet to come.

debates: Why no bone was to be broken: Clarke and Calvin give haste, Ellicott a symbol of unity, and Calvin explicitly refuses the reading that the bones represent an undiminished virtue in Christ.
Whether the closing formula belongs to this chapter or the next: Keil calls it a conclusion but concedes Abenezra’s point that such formulae also introduce what follows.
outliers: Clarke uses the first occurrence of the word law to argue that a nation’s penal justice is proportionate only where this revelation is acknowledged, and traces political upheaval to its absence.
Calvin declines a typological reading for the second time in this chapter, having earlier refused to explain why the flesh was roasted rather than boiled.
